claims.text: A multiscale simulation framework with bespoke interatomic potentials will predict exceptionally low phonon thermal conductivity in high-entropy alloys more accurately than traditional ab initio or empirical methods.
Bespoke interatomic potentials can be tuned to capture local chemical disorder in high-entropy alloys.
Chemical disorder enhances phonon scattering in high-entropy alloys.
Disorder-enhanced phonon scattering is a critical mechanism governing phonon thermal conductivity in these materials.
Explicitly representing disorder-enhanced phonon scattering will quantitatively improve prediction accuracy.
The target materials are equimolar or near-equimolar high-entropy alloys in a disordered solid-solution state.
Disordered equimolar or near-equimolar high-entropy alloys are typical of thermal-insulation applications.
The intervention is application of a multiscale computational framework using bespoke interatomic potentials.
The relevant temperature range extends from room temperature to moderately high temperatures under conditions where phonon conduction dominates heat transfer.
Local lattice distortions enhance phonon scattering.
Incorporating local chemical disorder into the interatomic-force description more accurately represents intrinsic disorder-induced vibrational dynamics.
Models that neglect detailed atomic-scale heterogeneity predict higher phonon thermal conductivity than the proposed framework.
The proposed framework will reduce prediction error by approximately 10–20% relative to current prediction models.
Standard ab initio and semi-empirical prediction methods do not fully incorporate the effects of chemical disorder.
Traditional methods have higher prediction errors or overestimate phonon thermal conductivity.
The approach is primarily applicable to chemically disordered equimolar or near-equimolar high-entropy alloys under phonon-dominated thermal transport.
The approach may not apply when alternative heat-transfer mechanisms prevail or local disorder is minimal.
Temperature-dependent anharmonic effects are not fully captured by the proposed framework.

A decisive benchmark would compare predicted and experimentally measured phonon thermal conductivities for matched HEAs over the relevant temperature range using both the proposed and traditional methods.
The hypothesis is falsified if the proposed method fails to achieve a statistically significant reduction of at least 10% in prediction error relative to traditional models.
